headline: Three imported style values merged onto one element fold into a single class: next-yak emits `className="yTV3SxX"` and drops the wrapper component entirely, running 1.44× its own no-fold lane.

microbench.why: Every module here exports declarations rather than a component, so all three land on one element and the only question is when the merge happens. `next-yak` answers at build time — the compiled output is `jsx("button", { className: "yTV3SxX" })`, the three imported values concatenated into one class and the `GhostPrimaryButton` wrapper removed, so it renders one fiber where `vanilla` renders two and joins three class strings per instance. That is worth 1.44× against its own `foldStatic: false` lane and 18% against the hand-written baseline. `cnfast` reaches 1.86M on a fast string join. The atomic lanes cannot fold a merge whose inputs cross a module boundary, so `stylex` runs `props()` through `styleq` for each of the 1,000 buttons, and `emotion` at 331,000 re-serializes the composed rules every time.

autocannon.why: Over HTTP the fold compounds: `next-yak` serves 1,798 req/s against 1,252 for its no-fold lane and 1,368 for `vanilla`. Work the compiler removed never enters the response path at all, while `styled-components` at 458 req/s and `emotion` at 315 run their serializer once per button per request.

attribution.why: SSR CPU shows where the win comes from. `next-yak` totals 0.557 ms with 0.222 ms of lib self-time and no component self-time whatsoever, because no wrapper component survives the build to be charged. `vanilla` totals 0.716 ms, 0.237 ms of it component self-time doing the template join. The runtime lanes climb by their serializer: `styled-components` books 1.73 ms of lib time inside a 2.24 ms render, `emotion` 2.61 ms inside 3.76 ms.

hydrate.why: Nine of fifteen lanes hydrate between 43.9 ms and 48.7 ms, because one button with a settled sheet leaves the client almost nothing to redo. `goober` at 139 ms, `styled-components` at 102 ms and `emotion` at 78.5 ms rebuild their sheets before React can attach.

top3.label: StyleX without CSS layers (:not() specificity hack)

inp.why: One click on one button puts thirteen lanes between 6.4 ms and 8.4 ms, inside each other's spread, so this axis does not separate them. `emotion` at 13.6 ms is the only lane whose interaction re-enters a serializer.

mount.why: Mounting 1,000 buttons keeps the render ordering but compresses it, since parse and layout are shared: `next-yak` leads at 65.7 ms against 70.6 ms for `vanilla`. `emotion` at 106 ms carries its sheet construction into the mount itself.

renderTiming.why: One style recalculation everywhere, costing between 0.122 ms and 0.180 ms. With one element per instance and identical DOM, the engine's work is the same no matter who wrote the class names.

payload.why: `next-yak-css` ships 3,078 gz B and `next-yak` 3,889 B, the difference being the 1,152 B `Yak` runtime the css-prop lane never loads. `vanilla` ships no JS at all. Everything else pays for a merge function or a full runtime: 3,478 B of JS for `stylex`, 10.6 kB for `tailwind-merge`, 13.5 kB for `styled-components`. `cnfast` totals 15.2 kB, almost all of it an 11.6 kB merge runtime for a page holding one button.

nsweep.why: At the largest size `next-yak` holds 1.66 ms while `next-yak-nofold` needs 2.63 ms, so folding keeps its 1.58× as the count grows rather than amortizing away. `emotion` reaches 12.2 ms, because per-instance serialization sets its slope.

crossCase: The Example `button-variants-nested` shown below is this exact ladder with one change: each module exports a JSX component instead of a style value. Same declarations, same three modules, same rendered element. Values fold across the module boundary and components do not, which drops `next-yak` from 2.12M to 1.19M renders/s and costs even hand-written `vanilla` 22%.
